message.reasoning_content:
Let me analyze this situation carefully.

The user's position: Aave V3 Ethereum Core, supplies WETH (~$1,000), no debt. So they're a supplier/lender of WETH.

Timeline of events:
1. 17:35 UTC: Kelp DAO rsETH bridge exploited, 116,500 rsETH (~$292M) drained via LayerZero cross-chain message spoofing.
2. 17:38-17:44: Attacker address supplied 52,999 rsETH to Aave V3 Core and borrowed 52,439.6 WETH (~$180M?) in e-mode near max LTV. WETH utilization jumped to 90.3%.
3. 18:21: Kelp paused rsETH token and related contracts.
4. 18:44: News reports Aave V3 suffering bad debt due to Kelp hack.
5. 19:03: Aave froze rsETH reserve.
6. 19:17-19:20: PeckShield, The Block confirm exploit ~$292M.
7. 19:20: USDT withdrawals $535M, utilization rising.
8. 19:21: Marc Zeller urges WETH suppliers to withdraw.
9. 19:36: Massive WETH withdrawals (231,870 WETH), utilization 97.33%, idle 75k.
10. 19:45: WETH utilization 99%, idle 25.5k.
11. 19:55: Aave official confirms rsETH markets frozen, Aave contracts not exploited.
12. 20:05: WETH utilization 99.7%, idle 9.2k falling to 13 WETH at 20:05. Essentially zero idle WETH.
13. 20:08: Stani confirms rsETH frozen, no borrowing power, Aave has no further exposure to rsETH.
14. 20:10: Kelp confirms pause.
15. 20:13: Cyvers confirms $293M exploit.
16. 20:29: PeckShield: attacker deposited rsETH into Aave, Compound, Euler, borrowed >$236M WETH debt.
17. 20:36: BeInCrypto: Aave WETH reserve carrying bad debt; partial withdrawals may only be possible after Umbrella backstop settles deficit.
18. 20:53: CoinDesk confirms.
19. 22:24: LlamaRisk: freezes initiated, all pools "safe and fully operational," incident scoped to rsETH.
20. 00:00: DeFiLlama hack entry: $293M.
21. 01:50: Lookonchain: bad debt on Aave, whales withdrawing ETH, ETH utilization 100%.
22. 01:50: Chain monitor: USDT utilization 99%, WETH 100% utilization, idle 0 since ~20:05.
23. 02:15 (current): WETH reserve FROZEN, WETH LTV set to 0 (liquidation threshold unchanged at 83%). Utilization 100%, idle 0.

Key question: What's the risk to a WETH supplier with ~$1,000 supplied, no debt?

Critical facts:
- The attacker borrowed ~$236M WETH against rsETH collateral that is now worthless/paused. This creates bad debt in the WETH reserve on Aave V3 Core. The bad debt means WETH suppliers' deposits are impaired — suppliers cannot be fully withdrawn; the deficit will be socialized or covered by Umbrella (Aave's safety module backstop).
- WETH utilization is 100% with idle = 0. This means there is literally no WETH liquidity to withdraw into. A supplier cannot withdraw right now — withdrawals would fail/revert due to insufficient liquidity.
- At 02:15, the WETH reserve has been frozen (new supply disabled, and typically freeze prevents new supply and borrowing but allows withdrawals and repayments). LTV set to 0 means WETH can't be used as collateral for new borrows (existing collateral status? Setting LTV to 0 typically prevents new collateral usage but liquidation threshold remains 83%, so existing collateral positions remain but can't borrow more).

Wait — actually, when a reserve is frozen on Aave, supply and borrow are disabled, but withdrawals and repayments are still allowed. So the user could still attempt to withdraw — but there's zero idle WETH, so withdrawal would fail.

So the position: $1,000 WETH supplied, no debt. The WETH reserve has bad debt from the attacker's position (borrowed $236M against rsETH collateral now frozen/worthless-ish). The deficit will be covered partially by Umbrella (Aave's backstop which caps coverage) and then socialized via bad debt deficit — suppliers bear losses pro-rata.

Actually, let me think about the magnitude. The attacker borrowed 52,439.6 WETH from Aave V3 Core (~$180M at ~$3,450/ETH? Actually $236M total across Aave, Compound, Euler per PeckShield). The rsETH collateral is frozen with zero borrowing power and rsETH itself is paused — its value is impaired (bridge drained 18% of supply; rsETH likely depegged significantly). Liquidating rsETH collateral: rsETH is paused, can it even be sold? The attacker's position has rsETH collateral worth maybe much less than the debt. Bad debt = debt minus recoverable collateral value.

So WETH suppliers on Aave V3 Core face a real loss: their deposits are impaired. The Umbrella safety module may cover some, but $180M+ bad debt likely exceeds the backstop, so suppliers will take a haircut (aTokens depeg or deficit socialized).

Also, liquidity: idle WETH = 0. Withdrawal is impossible right now even though the reserve is frozen (frozen allows withdrawals). So "exit" action can't actually execute... but the keeper can only propose an action; corridor limits enforce safety. The instruction says "you cannot move funds, only propose an action; the corridor limits enforce safety."

Hmm, but what's the right action? Options:
- exit: withdraw whole position now. But there's zero liquidity — withdrawal would fail. Still, proposing exit signals urgency; when liquidity returns (e.g., after repayments or deficit settlement), the keeper would exit. But exiting now is impossible; also, if withdrawals are processed pro-rata during deficit, exiting early might be advantageous (first-come-first-served on remaining liquidity?). Actually in Aave, when there's bad debt, withdrawals are limited by available liquidity. With 100% utilization and 0 idle, no one can withdraw. As borrowers repay or positions get liquidated, liquidity trickles back. There's a run dynamics: everyone tries to withdraw first.

Wait, but actually — can borrowers repay? The WETH reserve frozen means borrows disabled but repayments allowed. The attacker might repay? Unlikely. Liquidations of the attacker's rsETH position: rsETH is paused — can't be transferred/sold? Liquidation requires swapping rsETH... The rsETH reserve on Aave is frozen; liquidations can still occur on frozen reserves (liquidation of positions using frozen asset as collateral is allowed if health factor < 1). But selling rsETH for WETH — the frozen reserve prevents... actually liquidation swaps collateral asset to debt asset via the pool; if rsETH reserve is frozen, the swap might fail? In Aave V3, frozen reserves can still be used in liquidations? Hmm, there are nuances. Anyway.

The key decision: risk level and action.

Risk to the position: HIGH to CRITICAL. The user's $1,000 WETH deposit:
1. Faces impairment from bad debt (~$180M borrowed against worthless collateral in this market; deficit will be socialized across suppliers — with total WETH supplied maybe ~$1-2B? Actually WETH supplied on Aave V3 Core is on the order of 1M+ WETH (~$3.5B?). Hmm, let's estimate: idle was 280k WETH at 19:20 with utilization 90.6% → total supplied ≈ 280k/0.094 ≈ 3.0M WETH ≈ $10B? That seems too high. Actually utilization 90.67% means borrowed/supplied = 0.9067. Idle 280k is available liquidity = supplied - borrowed. If borrowed B and supplied S, B/S = 0.9067, S - B = 280k → S(1-0.9067) = 280k → S ≈ 3.0M WETH ≈ $10.4B at $3,450. Hmm, that's plausible-ish for Aave V3 Core WETH? Actually Aave V3 Core WETH supply is around 1.5-2M WETH historically (~$5-7B). Fine, order of millions of WETH.

Bad debt: attacker borrowed 52,439.6 WETH from Aave Core. Collateral: 52,999 rsETH. rsETH value: pre-hack ~$5,500 each ($292M/116,500 ≈ $2,506 each? Wait, 116,500 rsETH = $292M → $2,506/rsETH. Hmm, rsETH ~0.96 ETH? If ETH ~$2,600... but this is 2026 fictional. Let's not over-compute. 52,999 rsETH ≈ $133M collateral; borrowed 52,439.6 WETH ≈ $180M? That doesn't match e-mode near max LTV... Actually in e-mode rsETH/WETH, LTV maybe 90%+. If borrowed $180M, collateral would be ~$200M. Whatever — the numbers: borrowed 52,439.6 WETH. If WETH ≈ $3,450, that's $181M. Hmm, but CoinDesk says $292M for 116,500 rsETH → rsETH = $2,506. Then 52,999 rsETH = $133M collateral, borrowing $181M would be impossible. So maybe WETH ≈ $2,500 and borrowed ≈ $131M, collateral 52,999 rsETH ≈ $133M at pre-hack price — near max LTV ~98%? That's odd but it's fictional data. Anyway, roughly $130-180M borrowed against rsETH now impaired.

rsETH post-hack: paused, bridge drained 18% of supply. rsETH likely trades at a big discount (maybe 50-80% off). So collateral recoverable maybe $30-60M vs debt $130-180M → bad debt maybe $70-150M in the WETH reserve.

Total WETH supplied ~3M WETH (~$7.5B). Bad debt $100M / $7.5B ≈ 1.3% haircut. Hmm, that's meaningful but not catastrophic. But wait — Umbrella (safety module) covers first. Aave's safety module has limited funds. The BeInCrypto article says "partial withdrawals may only become possible after Aave's Umbrella backstop settles the deficit."

For a $1,000 position, expected loss maybe 1-3% ($10-30) if socialized. But the immediate problem: liquidity is zero; can't withdraw. And the reserve is now frozen — which signals Aave governance taking emergency action on WETH itself. Frozen reserve + LTV 0: suppliers can still withdraw (freeze doesn't block withdrawals), but there's no liquidity.

Also consider: is the user's WETH deposit itself at risk of total loss? No — WETH is the borrowed asset; bad debt socialization reduces aToken value slightly. The bigger risk is illiquidity: funds stuck until deficit resolved or borrowers repay. With 100% utilization and frozen reserve, borrow rate spikes (8.35%+ and rising) which incentivizes repayment... but borrowers can't be forced to repay quickly. Actually high rates attract deposits too, but supply is frozen — new deposits can't come in! That's important: freeze prevents new supply, so the only way liquidity returns is via repayments or liquidations. The attacker won't repay. Other WETH borrowers (real borrowers using other collateral) face rising rates and may repay. Also their positions: WETH LTV set to 0 means WETH collateral can't support new borrows; liquidation threshold unchanged 83% so existing WETH-collateral positions still work but as rates spike, some get liquidated, bringing... liquidations of WETH collateral sell WETH for debt assets — that drains WETH liquidity further? No wait: liquidation of a position with WETH collateral and, say, USDC debt: liquidator repays USDC debt and receives WETH (at discount). That takes WETH OUT of the pool (liquidator pulls WETH). Hmm, that reduces WETH in pool. Repayments of WETH debt add WETH back.

So liquidity recovery depends on WETH borrowers repaying. With borrow rate spiking (variable rate at 100% utilization can go very high, like 20-50%+), borrowers are incentivized to repay. Some will.

Now, what should the keeper do?

The position: $1,000 WETH supplied, no debt. Risk: the deposit is impaired (bad debt socialization) and illiquid (can't withdraw now). The reserve is frozen — a severe venue-level event.

Given the framework: "Staying put during a real incident can leave funds stuck or lost even when prices look normal (exploits, oracle faults, bad collateral, liquidity runs, pauses and freezes)."

This is exactly that scenario: bad collateral (rsETH), bad debt, liquidity run, pause and freeze. The position should exit. But exit is currently impossible (zero liquidity). Still, the action to propose: exit. The corridor limits enforce safety — if the exit tx would fail, the keeper system handles it. Proposing exit is the right signal: withdraw as soon as any liquidity is available.

Alternatively, "reduce_to_target"? No — for a supplier with bad debt socialization pending, you want out entirely, ASAP. Every hour at 100% utilization... actually being in the pool doesn't lose more per se; the deficit is set by the bad debt, socialized pro-rata at settlement. Exiting early avoids the haircut IF you can get out before deficit socialization. In Aave V3, bad debt is converted to deficit via Umbrella auction; aToken value drops for everyone remaining. If you withdraw before the deficit is realized, you avoid the loss. So there's a race: withdraw as liquidity frees up, before Umbrella settles deficit. That argues for exit ASAP.

But wait — there's a subtlety: with the reserve frozen, can suppliers withdraw? Yes, freeze allows withdrawals (only supply/borrow disabled). But zero idle WETH means withdrawal reverts. So the keeper should propose exit and retry as liquidity appears. The system says corridor limits enforce safety — presumably they'd queue it.

Hmm, but also consider: is exit even the right call given the loss is already locked in? The bad debt already exists — the attacker already borrowed the WETH. The deficit will be socialized. If the user stays, they eat pro-rata haircut. If they exit before settlement, they avoid it (assuming withdrawal at par). So exiting ASAP is value-maximizing. The race dynamics: everyone will try; liquidity comes from borrower repayments. First to withdraw at each liquidity event gets out at par.

Also note: the user's position is tiny ($1,000). Even a 2% haircut is $20. But gas costs to retry withdrawals... whatever, the framework wants risk management.

Risk level: critical? Let's calibrate. The venue (Aave V3 Core WETH reserve) is: frozen, 100% utilization, zero idle liquidity, carrying bad debt from a $293M exploit, with the deficit to be socialized. For a supplier, this is about as bad as it gets short of total loss: funds are stuck (cannot withdraw) and impaired (bad debt). I'd say "critical" is justified: funds effectively locked + impairment confirmed by multiple sources (BeInCrypto: "WETH pool is effectively impaired"; Lookonchain: "bad debt on Aave"; PeckShield: $236M debt).

Alternatively "high" with action exit. Hmm. The risk scale: low, elevated, high, critical. Critical typically = imminent/active loss of funds, venue compromised. Here: the Aave protocol itself is NOT exploited (officials confirm), but the WETH reserve is impaired and frozen, liquidity zero. The user cannot access funds. Bad debt socialization will directly reduce their deposit value. I think "critical" fits: active incident directly touching the position's reserve, funds stuck, confirmed bad debt.

Action: exit. Even though immediate withdrawal will fail due to zero liquidity, proposing exit is correct — the keeper should attempt/queue withdrawal and exit as soon as liquidity permits. The alternative "hold" would be wrong (waiting means eating the socialized deficit and remaining stuck). "reduce_light"/"reduce_to_target" are half-measures inappropriate when the reserve itself is impaired.

Wait, but should I consider that exit is impossible and therefore propose "hold" until liquidity returns? The prompt: "you cannot move funds, only propose an action; the corridor limits enforce safety." So the keeper proposes; limits enforce. Proposing exit is the correct intent. Also, some keepers would queue the withdrawal to execute when liquidity appears. I'll go with exit.

Let me double-check the "no debt" aspect: user supplies WETH, no debt. So user is a pure lender. Their risk: credit impairment of WETH reserve + illiquidity. Yes.

One more consideration: could this be a false alarm / noise? No — confirmed by Aave official, Stani, LlamaRisk, multiple security firms, DeFiLlama. The exploit is real ($293M). The bad debt in WETH reserve is reported by PeckShield, Lookonchain, BeInCrypto, and our own chain monitor showed the attacker borrowing 52,439.6 WETH. The freeze of WETH reserve at 02:15 is from our own chain monitor — highest confidence.

Also note O27: WETH LTV set to 0 — this means the user's WETH deposit no longer functions as collateral (can't borrow against it), though with no debt that matters less; but it also signals governance treating WETH reserve as distressed. Liquidation threshold unchanged at 83% — hmm, interesting: they kept LT so existing borrowers aren't instantly liquidated.

Decision: risk = critical, action = exit.

Reasons:
- Attacker's frozen rsETH collateral left ~$130-180M WETH debt unbacked in the same WETH reserve the user supplies; multiple sources confirm bad debt; deficit will be socialized onto suppliers (aToken impairment).
- WETH reserve frozen and LTV set to 0 by Aave governance/emergency mechanism — venue-level distress action directly on the user's asset.
- Utilization 100% with zero idle WETH since ~20:05 — withdrawals cannot execute; funds stuck; any liquidity that appears will be contested in a run (231,870 WETH already withdrawn).
- Exiting before Umbrella deficit settlement avoids the pro-rata haircut; propose exit and withdraw as soon as any liquidity is available.
